question: Which part of the cell hosts respiration?

response_a.text:
According to the source: “It takes place mainly in the mitochondria of the cell.” [1]

Sources:
[1] Source A

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen. It takes place mainly in the mitochondria of the cell. Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm and yields a small amount of ATP. The Krebs cycle then breaks pyruvate down and produces carbon dioxide and electron carriers. The electron transport chain uses those carriers to make most of the ATP and consumes oxygen.

Water is formed when oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain. Without oxygen, cells can use fermentation, which yields much less ATP. Muscle cells produce lactic acid during fermentation.

question: What forms at divergent boundaries?

response_a.text:
The cited material states: “At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms from rising magma.” [1]

Sources:
[1] Source A

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's outer shell is divided into large moving plates. The plates float on the hot, slowly flowing mantle beneath them. Heat from the Earth's interior drives convection currents in the mantle that move the plates. Plates move only a few centimetres each year.

At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms from rising magma. At convergent boundaries plates collide, and one plate may slide beneath the other in a process called subduction. Subduction produces deep ocean trenches and volcanic arcs. At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, which can cause earthquakes. Mountain ranges such as the Himalayas formed where two continental plates collided.

question: What does myelin do?

response_a.text:
The cited material states: “The axon of many neurons is wrapped in myelin, which speeds up the impulse.” [1]

Sources:
[1] Source A

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
Neurons are cells that carry electrical signals through the nervous system. A neuron receives signals through its dendrites and sends them along its axon. When a neuron is stimulated enough, it fires an electrical impulse called an action potential. The axon of many neurons is wrapped in myelin, which speeds up the impulse.

Neurons communicate with each other at junctions called synapses. When an impulse reaches the end of an axon, it releases chemicals called neurotransmitters. Neurotransmitters cross the synapse and bind to receptors on the next neuron. This binding can excite the next neuron or inhibit it. Repeated use of a synapse can strengthen it, which is one basis of learning and memory.

question: Which gas is released when water molecules are split?

response_a.text:
The cited material states: “Oxygen is released as a by-product when water molecules are split.” [1]

Sources:
[1] Source A

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the pigment chlorophyll. The light-dependent reactions capture sunlight and produce ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

Oxygen is released as a by-product when water molecules are split. Factors such as light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature limit the rate of photosynthesis. Plants store excess glucose as starch for later use. Photosynthesis in algae and some bacteria also supplies most of the oxygen in the atmosphere.

question: What is transpiration?

response_a.text:
Definition: The cited material states: “Plants also release water vapour into the air through transpiration.” [1]

Sources:
[1] Source A

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
The water cycle describes how water moves between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land. Heat from the sun causes water to evaporate from oceans, lakes and rivers. Plants also release water vapour into the air through transpiration. As the vapour rises it cools and condenses into clouds. When cloud droplets grow heavy they fall as rain, snow or hail.

Some precipitation runs over the surface into streams and rivers, a process called runoff. Other water soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. Groundwater can stay underground for thousands of years before it returns to the surface. Rivers eventually carry water back to the oceans, completing the cycle.

question: Where do photosynthesis and respiration each happen in the cell?

response_a.text:
According to the source: “Photosynthesis in algae and some bacteria also supplies most of the oxygen in the atmosphere.” [1] A different source says: “Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen.” [2] A different source says: “Plates move only a few centimetres each year.” [3]

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Source A
sources.text:
Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the pigment chlorophyll. The light-dependent reactions capture sunlight and produce ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

Oxygen is released as a by-product when water molecules are split. Factors such as light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature limit the rate of photosynthesis. Plants store excess glucose as starch for later use. Photosynthesis in algae and some bacteria also supplies most of the oxygen in the atmosphere.

sources.label: Source B
sources.title: Source B
sources.text:
Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen. It takes place mainly in the mitochondria of the cell. Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm and yields a small amount of ATP. The Krebs cycle then breaks pyruvate down and produces carbon dioxide and electron carriers. The electron transport chain uses those carriers to make most of the ATP and consumes oxygen.

Water is formed when oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain. Without oxygen, cells can use fermentation, which yields much less ATP. Muscle cells produce lactic acid during fermentation.

Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's outer shell is divided into large moving plates. The plates float on the hot, slowly flowing mantle beneath them. Heat from the Earth's interior drives convection currents in the mantle that move the plates. Plates move only a few centimetres each year.

At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms from rising magma. At convergent boundaries plates collide, and one plate may slide beneath the other in a process called subduction. Subduction produces deep ocean trenches and volcanic arcs. At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, which can cause earthquakes. Mountain ranges such as the Himalayas formed where two continental plates collided.

sources.text:
Neurons are cells that carry electrical signals through the nervous system. A neuron receives signals through its dendrites and sends them along its axon. When a neuron is stimulated enough, it fires an electrical impulse called an action potential. The axon of many neurons is wrapped in myelin, which speeds up the impulse.

Neurons communicate with each other at junctions called synapses. When an impulse reaches the end of an axon, it releases chemicals called neurotransmitters. Neurotransmitters cross the synapse and bind to receptors on the next neuron. This binding can excite the next neuron or inhibit it. Repeated use of a synapse can strengthen it, which is one basis of learning and memory.
